options.b: Generic: Ibuprofen. Class: NSAID. Primary use: Pain and inflammation.
options.c: Generic: Tramadol. Class: Opioid analgesic. Primary use: Moderate pain.
options.d: Generic: Hydrocodone/APAP. Class: Opioid + APAP. Primary use: Moderate pain (C-II).

ptcb-pharmacy-technician-mock-015.explanation: Norco is hydrocodone with acetaminophen (APAP), an opioid combination used for moderate pain. Hydrocodone combination products are DEA Schedule II, so refills are not allowed.

distractorExplanations.a: Oxycodone/APAP is Percocet, not Norco.
distractorExplanations.b: Ibuprofen is Motrin/Advil, an NSAID, not an opioid combination.
distractorExplanations.c: Tramadol is Ultram, not Norco.

options.b: Generic: Alendronate. Class: Bisphosphonate. Primary use: Osteoporosis. Key note: Take upright with a full glass of water.
options.c: Generic: Escitalopram. Class: SSRI. Primary use: Depression, GAD. Key note: Start low in elderly.
options.d: Generic: Famotidine. Class: H2 blocker. Primary use: GERD. Key note: Less acid suppression than a PPI.

distractorExplanations.a: Pantoprazole is Protonix, not Fosamax.
distractorExplanations.c: Escitalopram is Lexapro, not Fosamax.
distractorExplanations.d: Famotidine is Pepcid, not Fosamax.

options.a: Generic: Metoprolol. Class: Beta-blocker. Primary use: Hypertension, angina. Key note: Do not stop abruptly.
options.b: Generic: Metformin. Class: Biguanide. Primary use: Type 2 diabetes. Key note: Hold around iodinated contrast per protocol.
options.c: Generic: Nitrofurantoin. Class: Nitrofuran antibiotic. Primary use: Uncomplicated UTI. Key note: Take with food.
options.d: Generic: Spironolactone. Class: K-sparing diuretic. Primary use: HF, HTN. Key note: Hyperkalemia risk.

distractorExplanations.a: Metoprolol is Lopressor / Toprol XL, not Glucophage.
distractorExplanations.c: Nitrofurantoin is Macrobid, not Glucophage.
distractorExplanations.d: Spironolactone is Aldactone, not Glucophage.

options.a: High abuse potential; no refills allowed; examples: oxycodone, fentanyl, amphetamine salts.
options.b: Lower abuse potential than C-III; up to 5 refills in 6 months; examples: alprazolam, tramadol.
options.c: Moderate abuse potential; up to 5 refills in 6 months; examples: ketamine, testosterone, codeine ≤90 mg/unit combos.
options.d: No accepted medical use in the US; cannot be dispensed; examples: heroin, LSD.

ptcb-pharmacy-technician-mock-046.explanation: Schedule III drugs have moderate-to-low potential for physical dependence. Federal law allows up to 5 refills within 6 months if the prescriber authorizes them. Examples include ketamine, anabolic steroids such as testosterone, and products with no more than 90 mg of codeine per dosage unit.

distractorExplanations.a: That describes Schedule II: high abuse potential and no refills.
distractorExplanations.b: That describes Schedule IV, which has lower abuse potential than Schedule III.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes Schedule I: no accepted medical use in the US.

options.a: Grams of drug per 100 g of product; 1% = 1 g/100 g.
options.b: Grams of drug per 100 mL of solution; 1% w/v = 1 g/100 mL.
options.c: Milliliters of drug per 100 mL of solution; 1% = 1 mL/100 mL.
options.d: Milligrams of drug per 1 mL of solution; 1% = 1 mg/mL.

distractorExplanations.a: That is percent weight-in-weight (w/w), used for ointments and creams.
distractorExplanations.c: That is percent volume-in-volume (v/v), used for liquids mixed with liquids.
distractorExplanations.d: 1% w/v is 1 g per 100 mL, which equals 10 mg/mL, not 1 mg/mL.

options.a: (Volume × minutes) ÷ drop factor.
options.b: Volume ÷ (drop factor × minutes).
options.c: (Volume ÷ hours) × drop factor.
options.d: (Volume × drop factor) ÷ minutes.

distractorExplanations.a: Minutes belong in the denominator and the drop factor in the numerator.
distractorExplanations.b: The drop factor multiplies the volume; it does not divide it.
distractorExplanations.c: That gives drops per hour; divide by 60 to get drops per minute.

options.a: Add the labeled volume of the labeled diluent to reach the stated mg/mL.
options.b: Add any convenient volume of sterile water, then label the final mg/mL.
options.c: Fill the vial completely with diluent so no air space remains inside.
options.d: Inject the dry powder directly into the patient's IV fluid bag.

distractorExplanations.b: The diluent volume must follow the label; a different volume changes the concentration.
distractorExplanations.c: Filling the vial ignores the labeled volume and produces the wrong concentration.
distractorExplanations.d: Powder is reconstituted in its vial with the labeled diluent before any further dilution.

options.a: Review claims data after dispensing to find prescribing trends.
options.b: Screen for interactions and duplications before dispensing.
options.c: Monitor the patient's therapy while the drug is being taken.
options.d: Count controlled-substance inventory at least every two years.

distractorExplanations.a: Reviewing claims after dispensing is retrospective DUR.
distractorExplanations.c: Monitoring during therapy is concurrent DUR.
distractorExplanations.d: The biennial controlled-substance count is a DEA inventory rule, not DUR.

options.b: Only the customer must notify the Administrator, and only within 24 hours of the change
options.c: No filing is ever required if the agent moves directly to an affiliated bank or trust company
options.d: Only FINRA Arbitration must be notified; the state Administrator is never told of terminations

distractorExplanations.b: Customers have no filing duty when an agent's association with a firm ends.
distractorExplanations.c: Moving to an affiliate does not remove the prompt notice duty to the Administrator.
distractorExplanations.d: The Administrator must be notified; FINRA arbitration is a dispute forum, not a registration notice.

options.b: Administrative staff may solicit freely as long as they are paid only a salary and no commissions
options.c: Cold-calling to recommend stocks is allowed without registration if orders are limited to odd lots
options.d: Registration is required only after the employee completes 50 solicitations in a calendar year

distractorExplanations.b: How the employee is paid does not matter; soliciting and recommending securities requires agent registration.
distractorExplanations.c: Order size does not create an exclusion from agent registration.
distractorExplanations.d: There is no 50-solicitation threshold; registration is required before soliciting.

options.d: Intentional or reckless deception, misstatements, omissions, or schemes in securities dealings

options.a: An adviser registered with the SEC, or excluded from state registration by federal preemption (typically due to AUM or adviser type).
options.c: Any person in the business of advising others about securities for compensation, whether registered with a state or the SEC.

distractorExplanations.c: That is the general definition of an investment adviser, not the federal covered subset.

options.b: Policy rate (primary tool), reserve requirements, open market operations, and forward guidance.

options.d: Dividend irrelevance (M&M), bird-in-hand (investors prefer certain dividends), and tax preference (investors prefer lower-taxed capital gains).

options.c: Calendar (January), value (low P/B), size (small caps), momentum, and post-earnings drift: possible inefficiency or risk premia.

cfa-level-2-readiness-check-equity-002.prompt: In a two-stage dividend discount model, how is the terminal value at the end of the high-growth stage typically estimated?

options.a: By discounting each high-growth dividend at the risk-free rate and adding the results together
options.b: By applying the Gordon growth model at the end of the high-growth stage and discounting it back
options.c: By multiplying the current dividend by the long-run growth rate, with no discounting required
options.d: By using the book value of equity at the start of the forecast horizon as the terminal price

cfa-level-2-readiness-check-equity-002.explanation: In a two-stage DDM, each dividend in the high-growth stage is discounted individually. At the end of that stage the terminal value is estimated with the Gordon growth model, V_n = D_(n+1) / (r − g), and then discounted back to today at the required return on equity.

distractorExplanations.a: Dividends are discounted at the required return on equity, and summing them alone omits the terminal value.
distractorExplanations.c: The terminal value uses D_(n+1) / (r − g) and must be discounted to the present.
distractorExplanations.d: Book value is not the DDM terminal value; the model values expected future dividends.

options.a: Relying on the manager's reported IRR without reviewing cash-flow timing
options.b: Focusing on entry valuation multiples while ignoring the exit route
options.d: Assuming LPs have the same governance rights as public shareholders

distractorExplanations.a: IRR depends on cash-flow timing and can be managed; due diligence checks the drivers behind it.
distractorExplanations.b: Exit assumptions are central to private equity returns and must be tested, not ignored.
distractorExplanations.d: LP rights are set by the partnership agreement and differ from public shareholder rights.

options.a: Price-to-earnings on GAAP net income, including depreciation
options.c: Modified duration of the REIT's unsecured bond issues
options.d: Book value per share without marking properties to market

distractorExplanations.a: GAAP EPS is distorted by real estate depreciation, which is why FFO/AFFO are used.
distractorExplanations.c: Bond duration measures the rate sensitivity of debt, not the equity value of a REIT.
distractorExplanations.d: Book value uses depreciated historical cost; NAV marks properties to market.

options.b: Generate predictable dividend streams similar to utility stocks
options.c: Behave like investment-grade bonds with fixed coupons and maturities
options.d: Have no storage, transport, or roll costs affecting futures returns

distractorExplanations.b: Physical commodities produce no dividends or other cash flows.
distractorExplanations.c: Commodities have no coupons or maturity; their returns come from price, roll, and collateral yield.
distractorExplanations.d: Storage costs and roll yield are major drivers of commodity futures returns.

options.a: The underlying investment strategy and portfolio holdings
options.b: The auditor and administrator appointed for each class
options.c: The legal jurisdiction of the master fund's portfolio

distractorExplanations.a: Share classes of one fund hold the same portfolio; they differ in terms such as fees and liquidity.
distractorExplanations.b: A fund uses one auditor and administrator across its share classes.
distractorExplanations.c: All classes of a fund share the same master portfolio and its jurisdiction.

options.a: Spot prices exceed futures prices, so the curve slopes downward
options.b: Futures prices converge to zero as contracts approach expiry
options.c: All maturities trade at one price regardless of storage cost
options.d: Longer-dated futures trade above nearer-dated contracts and spot

distractorExplanations.a: A downward-sloping futures curve is backwardation.
distractorExplanations.b: Futures converge to the spot price at expiry, not to zero.
distractorExplanations.c: A flat curve is neither contango nor backwardation; storage costs usually push it upward.

options.b: The best single month of historical returns in the pitch book
options.c: Headline returns reported in the manager's marketing materials
options.d: Peer-group rankings from the most recent calendar year alone

distractorExplanations.b: One strong month says nothing about risk, fees, or repeatable return drivers.
distractorExplanations.c: Marketing returns are unaudited and selective; appraisal needs risk, liquidity, and fee analysis.
distractorExplanations.d: A single year of peer rankings ignores risk, liquidity, and fees.

options.a: Employer-sponsored, pre-tax account for eligible medical expenses; largely use-it-or-lose-it each plan year.
Cost-sharing percentage the insured pays after the deductible is met.
options.b: Fixed dollar amount the insured pays for a covered service, such as a visit.
options.c: A health condition that existed before the policy's effective date.

distractorExplanations.a: That describes coinsurance.
distractorExplanations.b: That describes a copayment.

options.b: Hospital inpatient room and board, skilled nursing, and hospice (the Part A core)
options.c: Outpatient prescription drugs purchased through a private stand-alone drug plan
options.d: Long-term custodial nursing home care for as long as the beneficiary needs it

distractorExplanations.b: Inpatient hospital, skilled nursing, and hospice care are Medicare Part A benefits.
distractorExplanations.c: Stand-alone prescription drug plans are Medicare Part D.
distractorExplanations.d: Medicare does not cover long-term custodial care.

options.c: Term coverage whose death benefit stays level for the whole term

options.a: Permanent coverage with guaranteed cash value growth, like whole life
options.b: Monthly disability income if the insured cannot work due to illness
options.c: A savings account with policy loans available from the first day
options.d: Pure death benefit protection for a set period, with no cash value

distractorExplanations.a: Guaranteed cash value belongs to permanent insurance such as whole life, not term.
distractorExplanations.b: Replacing income during disability is disability income insurance.
distractorExplanations.c: Term has no cash value, so it has nothing to borrow against.

options.b: Any two people, even strangers with no financial or family relationship
options.c: The insured and the insurer's underwriting department at issue
options.d: The writing agent and the underwriter at the time of the claim

distractorExplanations.b: Strangers lack insurable interest; allowing it would turn insurance into a wager.
distractorExplanations.c: The insurer's underwriters are not the parties who need an insurable interest.
distractorExplanations.d: The agent and underwriter are not parties who must have an insurable interest in the insured.

options.a: Whole life is permanent with cash value; term is temporary pure protection
options.b: Whole life pays a death benefit only if the insured dies before age 65
options.c: Term always builds guaranteed cash value faster than whole life does
options.d: Whole life is available only as group coverage through an employer

distractorExplanations.b: Whole life pays whenever death occurs while the policy is in force, typically to age 100 or 121.
distractorExplanations.c: Term insurance builds no cash value.
distractorExplanations.d: Whole life is commonly sold as individual coverage.

options.a: The insurer's right to contest the policy after ~2 years in force
options.b: The insurer's right to raise premiums after the policy is issued
options.c: The owner's right to change beneficiaries once the insured has died
options.d: The owner's right to cancel the policy during the free-look period

distractorExplanations.b: Premium guarantees are set by the policy, not by the incontestability clause.
distractorExplanations.c: Beneficiary rights vest at death; this is unrelated to incontestability.
distractorExplanations.d: Cancelling for a refund is the free-look provision.

options.a: Premiums that start high and decrease to zero after the first year
options.c: A death benefit that is payable only if the insured reaches age 100
options.d: Coverage limited to accidental death, with premiums fixed for life

distractorExplanations.a: Graded premium policies start low and increase; premiums do not drop to zero.
distractorExplanations.c: The death benefit is payable at death while in force, not only at age 100.
distractorExplanations.d: Graded premium whole life covers death from any cause, not only accidents.

options.a: Converting the policy's cash value into disability income coverage
options.b: Surrendering the policy and forfeiting all accumulated cash value
options.c: Keeping the full death benefit for a limited term with no premiums

distractorExplanations.a: Nonforfeiture options do not convert life coverage into disability income.
distractorExplanations.b: Nonforfeiture laws exist precisely so the owner does not forfeit accumulated cash value.
distractorExplanations.c: Full face amount for a limited period is the extended term option.

options.a: Death rates by age (and often sex) observed in insured populations
options.b: Historical total returns of the insurer's general account investments
options.c: Frequency and severity of property losses by construction type
options.d: Rates of sickness and disability by age, used for health insurance

distractorExplanations.b: Investment returns affect pricing but are not what a mortality table measures.
distractorExplanations.c: Property loss data is used in property insurance, not life mortality tables.
distractorExplanations.d: Sickness and disability rates are morbidity tables.

options.a: Medical records from the applicant's physician, used to assess insurability
options.b: The agent's written summary of the applicant's answers and lifestyle
options.c: A consumer reporting agency's report on the applicant's character and habits
options.d: Results of the paramedical exam performed by a contracted examiner

distractorExplanations.b: The agent's report is a field underwriting document, not an APS.
distractorExplanations.c: A third-party report on character and habits is an inspection (consumer) report.
distractorExplanations.d: A paramedical exam is performed by the insurer's examiner, not the applicant's own physician.

options.a: Life insurance pricing based on death rates at each age
options.b: Auto collision frequency by driver age and vehicle type
options.c: Disability and health insurance, predicting sickness and injury rates
options.d: Asset allocation of the insurer's investment portfolio

distractorExplanations.a: Death rates by age are mortality tables.
distractorExplanations.b: Auto loss frequency is property and casualty rating data.
distractorExplanations.d: Portfolio allocation is an investment decision, not a morbidity table use.

options.a: Insurers decline applicants based on race or national origin
options.b: Healthy people buy more coverage than they need to reduce taxes
options.c: Agents steer clients toward the insurer paying the highest commission
options.d: Higher-risk people seek or keep coverage more than lower-risk people

distractorExplanations.a: That is unfair discrimination, which is prohibited; it is not anti-selection.
distractorExplanations.b: Anti-selection is about higher-risk people seeking coverage, not healthy people over-buying.
distractorExplanations.c: Commission-driven steering is an ethics issue, not anti-selection.

options.a: The share of each premium the agent keeps as commission
options.b: The maximum loss the insurer keeps before reinsurance applies
options.c: The percentage of claims the insurer pays within 30 days
options.d: The minimum capital a state requires the insurer to hold

distractorExplanations.a: Agent commission is unrelated to how much risk the insurer retains.
distractorExplanations.c: Claim payment speed is a service measure, not a retention limit.
distractorExplanations.d: Minimum capital is a solvency requirement, not a retention limit.

options.a: Ownership rights in the policy to another party
options.b: The agent's right to renewal commissions on the policy
options.c: The insurer's obligation to a state guaranty association
options.d: The insured's medical history to a new insurer for underwriting

distractorExplanations.b: Agent commissions are not policy ownership rights and are not assigned by the owner.
distractorExplanations.c: Guaranty association obligations belong to insurers, not to policy assignments.
distractorExplanations.d: Assignment transfers policy rights, not medical records.

options.a: Policy loan interest to reduce the outstanding death benefit
options.b: Dividends to buy additional paid-up whole life insurance
options.c: Surrender charges to buy a one-year term insurance rider
options.d: Premium waivers to extend coverage during a disability

distractorExplanations.a: Loan interest reduces values; paid-up additions increase coverage.
distractorExplanations.c: Buying one-year term with dividends is the one-year term dividend option, and surrender charges are not used.
distractorExplanations.d: Continuing coverage during disability is the waiver of premium rider.

options.a: The first of the two insureds dies, leaving the survivor
options.b: Either insured becomes disabled and cannot pay premiums
options.c: The second of the two insureds dies; often used for estate taxes
options.d: The policy's cash value reaches the face amount at maturity

distractorExplanations.a: Paying at the first death describes a first-to-die (joint life) policy.
distractorExplanations.b: Disability of an insured does not trigger a life insurance death benefit.
distractorExplanations.d: Cash value reaching face amount is policy endowment, not a survivorship death benefit.

options.a: Must be strictly complied with; a breach can void coverage
options.b: Are statements believed true to the best of the applicant's knowledge
options.c: Apply only to the payment of dividends on participating policies
options.d: Are oral promises by the agent that are not part of the contract

distractorExplanations.b: Statements true to the best of the applicant's knowledge are representations.
distractorExplanations.c: Warranties are not limited to policy dividends.
distractorExplanations.d: Warranties are part of the contract, not oral agent promises.

options.a: No paperwork, as long as the client verbally agrees to the change
options.b: Written approval from the existing insurer before the new policy issues
options.c: Disclosure forms comparing existing and proposed coverage, per state rules
options.d: The agent to wait until the old policy lapses before taking an application

distractorExplanations.a: Replacement rules require written disclosure and acknowledgment, not verbal agreement.
distractorExplanations.b: The existing insurer is notified, but its approval is not required.
distractorExplanations.d: Letting the old policy lapse first could leave the client uninsured; rules require disclosure, not a lapse.

options.a: Comparing policies side by side with full and accurate disclosure
options.b: Transferring part of a risk from one insurer to another insurer
options.c: Offering a client part of the commission to induce a sale
options.d: Inducing a policy replacement through misrepresentation

distractorExplanations.a: An accurate, fully disclosed comparison is legitimate, not twisting.
distractorExplanations.b: Transferring risk between insurers is reinsurance.
distractorExplanations.c: Sharing commission to induce a sale is rebating.

options.a: At issue for life insurance; at the time of loss for property
options.b: At claim payment only, for every line of insurance
options.c: At policy surrender or maturity, for life insurance
options.d: At both issue and death for life, never for property

distractorExplanations.b: Timing differs by line: life at issue, property at the time of loss.
distractorExplanations.c: Life insurable interest is required at issue, not at surrender or maturity.
distractorExplanations.d: Life insurable interest need not exist at death, and property requires it at the time of loss.

options.a: Replaces the underlying policy with new terms for the holder
options.b: Summarizes coverage but does not change the policy contract
options.c: Extends coverage limits beyond those stated in the policy
options.d: Is issued by the state insurance department to prove licensing

distractorExplanations.a: A certificate evidences coverage; it does not replace or amend the policy.
distractorExplanations.c: A certificate cannot grant more coverage than the policy provides.
distractorExplanations.d: Certificates of insurance are issued by insurers or agents, not the state regulator.

options.a: Free lifetime health coverage after any voluntary or involuntary job loss
options.b: Automatic Medicare enrollment in place of employer group coverage
options.c: Unlimited continuation of group coverage at the employee's old premium
options.d: Former employees to keep group health coverage temporarily at their own cost

distractorExplanations.a: COBRA is temporary and the former employee pays the premium.
distractorExplanations.b: COBRA continues the employer group plan; it is not Medicare enrollment.
distractorExplanations.c: COBRA is time-limited (typically 18–36 months) and the person pays up to 102% of the full premium.

options.a: The fixed amount paid each time the insured visits a doctor
options.b: The amount the insured pays before the plan starts sharing costs
options.c: The most the insured pays for covered care in a plan year
options.d: The percentage of costs shared with the insurer after coverage begins

distractorExplanations.a: A fixed amount per visit is a copayment.
distractorExplanations.c: The annual cap on insured spending is the out-of-pocket maximum.
distractorExplanations.d: Percentage cost sharing after the deductible is coinsurance.

options.a: Are required for all individual policies during the first 12 months
options.b: Apply only when the applicant had a gap in coverage over 63 days
options.c: Are prohibited in ACA-compliant plans for plan years since 2014
options.d: May be applied for life to any condition diagnosed before enrollment

distractorExplanations.a: The ACA prohibits pre-existing condition exclusions; they are not required.
distractorExplanations.b: The 63-day gap rule came from pre-ACA HIPAA portability, which the ACA superseded.
distractorExplanations.d: Lifetime exclusions for pre-existing conditions are prohibited in ACA-compliant plans.
